title: Sequences and series
note: A series converges when its partial sums approach a finite limit. If the terms do not go to 0, the series diverges; if they do, you still need a test. A geometric series Σ arⁿ (a ≠ 0) converges to a/(1 − r) exactly when |r| < 1. Taylor series write a function as a power series with coefficients f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n!.

read.title: Adding infinitely many numbers
text: An infinite series a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + ⋯ has a value only if its partial sums, the totals after n terms, settle toward a finite limit. The series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ⋯ does: each new term covers half of the remaining distance to 2, so the sum is 2. This is a geometric series, where each term is the previous one times a fixed ratio r. Geometric series converge exactly when |r| < 1, to the first term divided by 1 − r.

Terms shrinking to zero is necessary but not enough. The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ⋯ has terms that go to zero, yet its partial sums grow without bound. Tests such as the integral, comparison, ratio, and alternating series tests decide convergence in cases like these.

Power series extend the idea to functions. A Taylor series centered at 0 matches a function's value and all of its derivatives at 0, using the coefficient f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)/n! for xⁿ. Because every derivative of eˣ equals 1 at 0, its series is the sum of xⁿ/n!, which converges for every x. Sine and cosine give alternating series using only odd or only even powers. Truncating a Taylor series gives a polynomial that approximates the function near the center.

q.q: When does a series have a finite sum?
o: Whenever its terms go to zero
Whenever it has a ratio less than 2
When its partial sums approach a finite limit

q.q: What does the harmonic series show?
o: Every series with positive terms diverges
Terms going to zero do not guarantee convergence

q.q: Why is the Taylor series of eˣ the sum of xⁿ/n!?
o: Every derivative of eˣ equals 1 at 0
